name: ARO-INHBE
lead: ARO-INHBE is an investigational RNA interference (RNAi) therapy aimed at the INHBE gene, which encodes a liver-derived protein involved in fat distribution. It is being tested in people with obesity, with and without type 2 diabetes, and in a planned trial in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). It is not approved for any use anywhere.[1][2]

The only public information about the compound is its clinical trial registrations. A first-in-human Phase 1/2 study in adults with obesity began in December 2024 and is active but no longer recruiting, with an enrollment of 190.[1] A Phase 2 MASH trial of 252 adults is registered as not yet recruiting, with a start date of September 2026.[2] No results have been posted in the sources reviewed.

Interest in INHBE-targeting drugs in appearance communities centres on the idea of reducing fat while preserving muscle, a theme discussed for other drugs in the same class. No published human data on ARO-INHBE show whether it does this.

paras: One Phase 1/2 first-in-human trial (NCT06700538) is registered in adults with obesity with or without type 2 diabetes, with 190 participants; it started on 4 December 2024 and its status is active, not recruiting.[1] A Phase 2 trial (NCT07859813) in adults with MASH, planned for 252 participants and a September 2026 start, is registered as not yet recruiting.[2] No peer-reviewed results have been identified in the sources reviewed.

The registered programme spans obesity and a liver disease indication, indicating that the developer is exploring more than one use. Whether the compound changes fat distribution, body weight or liver fat in humans has not been reported in the sources reviewed.[1][2]

card.summary: An experimental RNAi drug against INHBE aimed at fat distribution; only early trial registrations exist so far.
card.note: Investigational only; no published human results.

quick.overview:
ARO-INHBE is an experimental RNA interference drug that targets the INHBE gene. It is in early clinical trials for obesity and is planned for a trial in fatty liver disease (MASH).

No results have been published, so its effects on fat, weight or muscle in people are unknown.
quick.mechanism: RNAi drugs reduce the production of a specific protein by silencing its gene. Here the target is INHBE, a gene linked to how fat is distributed in the body.
quick.risks: Safety in humans has not been reported. The drug is investigational and not available by prescription.
